queries.query_text: intratumoral inosine concentration mass spectrometry solid tumor

Are there prospective clinical studies measuring absolute intratumoral concentrations of inosine or short-chain fatty acids in human solid tumors and correlating these levels with immune checkpoint inhibitor response?

still_missing: This review does not report absolute physiological concentrations (e.g., μmol/g or μM) of inosine or SCFAs inside the human tumor microenvironment. It references associations in plasma and fecal samples but does not describe paired tumor tissue and serum/stool measurements from prospective human studies with specific quantitative data. The success criterion requiring identified prospective human studies with absolute tissue concentrations remains open.
usable_content: Section 6.3 identifies microbiome-derived metabolites, specifically short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and inosine, as candidate blood-accessible biomarkers associated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor outcomes. The authors note that higher concentrations of fecal and plasma SCFAs were associated with longer progression-free survival in patients treated with nivolumab or pembrolizumab, and preclinical studies suggest inosine enhances checkpoint blockade response. The text explicitly categorizes these markers as exploratory, highlighting confounding factors such as diet, antibiotic exposure, geography, and host metabolism that influence circulating metabolite concentrations. ['Explicit statement that human studies reporting spatial redistribution of inosine across intestinal compartments are currently missing, with most data derived from bulk metabolomic analysis.', 'Statement that no human studies have longitudinally tracked inosine levels or purine metabolic flux from colitis through dysplasia to established CRC.', 'Reference to a Phase-2 clinical trial (n=172 mixed solid tumors) evaluating inosine (0.2 g orally three times/day) as an adjunct to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors and chemotherapy, noting mild efficacy enhancement but lacking separate CRC-specific reporting (n=10 within digestive system group n=55).', 'Mechanistic evidence from preclinical models (germ-free mice, MC38/CT26 cells) showing microbial inosine (e.g., from Bifidobacterium pseudolongum) enhances ICI efficacy via A2A receptor-dependent T cell activation and IFN-γ release.', "Description of inosine's dual role: promoting anti-tumor immunity (Th1 differentiation, M1 macrophage polarization) versus supporting tumor metabolism (alternative carbon source, EMT promotion via LACC1 enzyme).", 'Identification of specific inosine-producing taxa (Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, Lactobacillus johnsonii/reuteri) and host enzymes (ADA, LACC1) regulating inosine availability.'] This study identifies inosine and short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) as key microbiota-derived metabolites influencing immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response. It reports that Bifidobacterium pseudolongum-derived inosine improves antitumor actions via activation of adenosine A2A receptors on T cells, citing preclinical evidence (Mager et al. 2020). For SCFAs, it notes that increased fecal propionic acid in anti-PD-1 patients correlates with increased antitumor responses and prolonged survival (Botticelli et al. 2020), while increased serum butyrate in anti-CTLA-4 patients links to poor outcomes (Coutzac et al. 2020a, b). Mechanisms described include SCFA-mediated histone deacetylase (HDAC) suppression and G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) activation. The text distinguishes between metabolite effects in different treatment contexts (anti-PD-1 vs. anti-CTLA-4) and compartments (fecal vs. serum).
